name: DIY peptide injections

lead: DIY peptide injections refers to people giving themselves injections of peptides such as growth-hormone secretagogues, BPC-157 or copper peptides outside clinical supervision. Users pursue outcomes that affect appearance: leaner body composition, muscle gain, faster recovery, skin or hair changes.

Most of these peptides are not approved drugs. The FDA has published safety concerns about several that have been nominated for compounding, including immunogenicity and limited or no human safety data.

paras: Users describe obtaining peptides in vial form, reconstituting and injecting them, often in stacks. This wiki does not provide dosing, sourcing or injection instructions.

The FDA lists immunogenicity risks and, for some peptides, reported serious adverse events or no human exposure data. Products bought outside regulated pharmacy channels may vary in purity and content. Anyone considering such compounds is generally advised to discuss them with a clinician.

chain: Claimed effects on fat, muscle, recovery or skin
angle.text: Users inject peptides hoping for fat loss, muscle, recovery or skin and hair effects. Human data are limited for most of them.

lead: DIY peptide injections describes the practice of self-injecting peptides at home, outside prescription oversight. Peptides commonly named in this context include growth-hormone secretagogues such as ipamorelin and CJC-1295, the healing-associated BPC-157 and TB-500, melanotan II and GHK-Cu.[1]

People use them to pursue appearance-relevant goals: body-composition change, muscle, tendon and joint recovery that supports training, skin quality, hair or tanning. The wiki's detailed compound entries describe each.

The US FDA has reviewed several of these substances for compounding and published concerns. It places GHRP-2, GHRP-6, ipamorelin acetate and kisspeptin-10 in a category with safety risks, citing immunogenicity and, for some, serious adverse events, and lists BPC-157, TB-500, CJC-1295, melanotan II and others among nominated substances that were withdrawn, noting limited or no human safety data.[1]
infobox: Ipamorelin, CJC-1295, BPC-157, TB-500, melanotan II, GHK-Cu

paras: The practice involves peptides sold as lyophilised powders from research-chemical vendors or obtained through compounding, then self-administered. The wiki does not give dosing, preparation or sourcing details.

The FDA's page on bulk drug substances lists immunogenicity risk for several peptides. It notes that ipamorelin has a literature report linking intravenous use to serious adverse events, including death, that CJC-1295 has reports of increased heart rate and vasodilation, and that melanotan II case reports describe melanoma and other serious events.[1] For BPC-157 and TB-500 the agency says safety information is limited or absent.[1]

Beyond drug effects, general risks of non-clinical injection include contamination and product variability; these are considered by clinicians and regulators rather than specific to any one peptide.[1]
No studies found on DIY use as a practice. Individual peptides have separate research profiles, covered in their own entries.

timeline.event: FDA adds GHRP-2, GHRP-6, ipamorelin acetate and kisspeptin-10 to its category of compounding substances with safety risks (September 29).[1]
